extract:
Boards of Canada are a Scottish electronic duo composed of brothers Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin, based for much of their career in rural Pendland, near Edinburgh. Active since the late 1980s, though they only began releasing music publicly in the mid-1990s, the pair became central figures in the wave of melodic, texture-focused electronic music that emerged from the United Kingdom in the wake of Aphex Twin and Autechre. They took their name from the National Film Board of Canada, whose educational documentaries from the 1970s — with their grainy film stock, synthesizer scores, and earnest narration — shaped the nostalgic, slightly uncanny atmosphere that would define their sound.

The brothers grew up partly in Canada before settling in Scotland, and as teenagers played in a larger collective called Hexagon Sun, which later became the name of their home studio and informal creative circle. Their earliest self-released cassettes and the limited 1996 EP Twoism circulated in small numbers before catching the attention of Sean Booth of Autechre, who helped bring them to the Skam label in Manchester. Their Skam EP Hi Scores in 1996 established the template: warm, detuned analog synthesizers, hip-hop-derived broken beats, half-buried children's voices, and melodies that felt simultaneously sunlit and decayed.

Their debut full-length, Music Has the Right to Children, was released in 1998 jointly by Warp and Skam and became one of the defining electronic albums of its era. Tracks like Roygbiv, Aquarius, and Turquoise Hexagon Sun cemented an aesthetic that critics often described as hauntological years before that term entered wider music writing. The follow-up, Geogaddi, arrived in 2002 with a darker, more numerologically obsessive bent, layered with references to cults, the Branch Davidians, and occult symbolism. The Campfire Headphase in 2005 leaned more heavily on processed guitar textures, and after a long silence, Tomorrow's Harvest in 2013 — preceded by an elaborate scavenger-hunt promotional campaign involving cryptic Record Store Day twelve-inches — offered a colder, more cinematic, dystopian sound indebted to John Carpenter and 1970s science fiction scoring.

Throughout their career, Boards of Canada have remained tied to Warp Records, sharing that roster with contemporaries like Autechre, Aphex Twin, and Plaid, and their influence radiated well beyond the IDM scene that initially housed them. The hypnagogic pop and vaporwave movements of the late 2000s and 2010s drew heavily on their handling of nostalgia and tape degradation, and artists ranging from Oneohtrix Point Never to Tycho have cited them as touchstones. Press appearances have been famously rare; the brothers grant few interviews and almost never perform live, a reticence that has only amplified the mystique around their releases.

As of the mid-2020s, Boards of Canada have not released a new studio album since Tomorrow's Harvest, and they remain characteristically silent about future plans, though Warp has reissued portions of their catalog on vinyl. Their legacy is by now well secured: Music Has the Right to Children regularly appears on best-of-decade and best-of-genre lists, and the duo's particular fusion of memory, melody, and analog warmth continues to shape how successive generations of electronic producers think about emotion in instrumental music.
title: Boards of Canada
